lesson.title: Measuring the Distance Between Wave Crests
lesson.summary: Wavelength is the physical distance between successive identical points on a wave, such as crest to crest, and it is the property that distinguishes radio waves from visible light from gamma rays across the electromagnetic spectrum.
lesson.body:
Light, along with every other form of electromagnetic radiation, travels as a wave, and like any wave it has a shape that repeats over and over as it moves through space. Wavelength, given the symbol lambda, is the distance between two successive corresponding points on that repeating wave, most commonly measured crest to crest or trough to trough. It is a straightforward physical length, and like any length it is measured in distance units: meters for very long waves, but often nanometers (billionths of a meter) or even picometers for the short wavelengths relevant to visible light and beyond.

You already know that the electromagnetic spectrum arranges every type of electromagnetic radiation, from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X rays, and gamma rays, along a single continuous scale. Wavelength is one of the two properties (frequency is the other) that defines where a given wave sits on that scale. Radio waves have enormous wavelengths, from about a meter to many kilometers. Visible light occupies a comparatively tiny sliver of the spectrum, roughly 400 to 700 nanometers, with violet light near the short end and red light near the long end. Gamma rays sit at the opposite extreme, with wavelengths shorter than a picometer, smaller than an atomic nucleus.

Every type of electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed in a vacuum, the speed of light, approximately 3.00 times 10 to the 8th meters per second, usually written as c. That fixed speed links wavelength to frequency through the equation c = lambda times nu, where nu is frequency. Because c is constant, wavelength and frequency must trade off against each other: waves with a longer wavelength necessarily have a lower frequency, and waves with a shorter wavelength necessarily have a higher frequency. This inverse relationship is not a coincidence; it falls directly out of the fact that all electromagnetic waves cover the same fixed distance, c, in one second, so a wave with longer individual cycles fits fewer of them into that same second.

Wavelength also connects directly to energy, which is the detail that matters most for chemistry. The energy of a single photon of light is given by E = hc / lambda, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 times 10 to the negative 34th joule seconds. Because wavelength sits in the denominator, shorter wavelength light carries more energy per photon, and longer wavelength light carries less. This is exactly why ultraviolet light, with wavelengths shorter than visible light, carries enough energy per photon to damage skin cells and DNA, while the much longer wavelengths of radio waves carry too little energy per photon to do comparable damage.

Within the visible range, this energy relationship is something you can observe directly: violet light, near 400 nanometers, has a noticeably shorter wavelength and higher energy per photon than red light, near 700 nanometers. This same wavelength dependence underlies atomic emission spectra, the specific colors of light that atoms emit when electrons drop from a higher energy orbital to a lower one, a topic that connects wavelength directly back to the orbital energy structure you spent this whole unit building.
